## What Is Offboarding Automation and Access Revocation?


When an employee leaves your company, their access to every SaaS application should disappear immediately. That's the straightforward goal of offboarding automation and access revocation. In reality, most companies handle this through a chaotic mix of spreadsheets, Slack messages, and hoping someone remembers to revoke that old Figma account.


Automated deprovisioning removes user access across all systems when employees leave or change roles, executing this process without manual intervention. Instead of your team logging into 40 different applications to disable accounts, the system handles revocation automatically. The moment an employee's last day hits in your HRIS, their accounts get deactivated across Google Workspace, AWS, Salesforce, and every other tool they touched.


Manual offboarding falls apart once you pass 20 employees. You're juggling too many tools, too many permissions, and too many people who need to take action. An HR person creates a ticket, you check a spreadsheet of applications, then you either handle each revocation yourself or ping tool owners who may take days to respond. Meanwhile, that departed employee still has access to your company's data, cloud infrastructure, or customer information.


The security risk is obvious but worth stating plainly. Every hour a former employee retains access to your systems creates a potential breach. Whether they left on good terms or bad, that open access creates liability.[Former employees cause many data breaches](https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/dbir/) , either through intentional misuse or simply because their credentials get compromised after they leave. If you're working toward SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification, auditors will ask you to prove how quickly you revoke access and whether any accounts slip through the cracks.


## Buyer Criteria When Assessing Offboarding and Software Revocation Tools


We pulled data from conversations with 100+ buying committees looking to automate offboarding, these were the five criteria that mattered most:


**One action that removes access everywhere:** Buyers wanted to stop removing people tool by tool, emailing team leads and chasing app owners to confirm. They wanted one click or the end date in the HRIS to start removal in every app at once. No ticket creation, no Slack reminder, no manual intervention.


**Coverage not limited by SCIM & APIs:** SCIM and API connectors only cover a fraction of the apps a typical company uses. Most teams stall when they learn that getting SCIM in Figma or Notion means an Enterprise upgrade that costs thousands of dollars a year. So even teams with Okta, or an HR and IT platform like Rippling, still had a long tail of apps they offboarded by hand. We counted how many of your typical applications each tool can actually automate, not how many appear on their "supported apps" page.


**Seeing the whole footprint, shadow apps included:** Buyers wanted the full list of what a leaver had access to, including tools IT never approved. Without it, leftover accounts turn up months later, often during an access review. We checked whether each tool finds these[hidden Shadow IT applications](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/shadow-it-tools-compared-buyers-guide) on its own.


**Knowing it actually finished in each app:** Buyers wanted confirmation that the account is gone in every app, without logging into each one to check. That includes the apps someone still removes by hand. Disabling an account in your IdP doesn't kill active browser sessions, so "suspended in Okta" isn't the same as done.


**Proof for the auditor:** Buyers working toward[SOC 2](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/detailed-guide-to-soc-2-access-reviews) or ISO 27001 need timestamped proof of what was removed and when. Some have promised their auditor that access is removed within 24 hours of someone leaving. An exportable record saves you from collecting screenshots app by app.

## Deel IT


A first place HR and Operations teams often look is extending their HR platform with an IT add-on module. It builds on a tool they already know. We chose Deel IT for this comparison, but most of these HR IT modules work in a similar way (Rippling IT is another well-known one). Deel IT adds laptops, device security, IT support and app access to Deel, all tied to the same employee records.


### What It Is


Deel IT is Deel's IT product line. App access sits in its Access Management feature. Deel says it is not an identity provider. Instead it syncs with the one you already run: Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace, Okta or JumpCloud. Deel holds the HR data that decides who gets what. Your IdP does the provisioning.


### What It Covers


-


**Access Groups:** You build groups from HR data like role, team or location. Each group maps to a set of apps, so a new designer can get Slack, Figma and Notion at once.


-


**Offboarding:** Deel says a deactivated worker is typically moved to an offboarded group in your IdP, "which revokes access to all applications." You choose how many days before or after the last day access ends.


-


**Workflows:** Deel's workflow builder can add approval rules for granting and removing app access.


For a closer look at how this runs day to day, see our guide to[automating SaaS provisioning with Deel](https://www.accessowl.com/blog/deel-hris-tools-to-automate-saas-provisioning) .


### Limitations


-


**App coverage stops at your IdP:** Deel IT only reaches apps your IdP can provision. Google Workspace, for example, automates provisioning for about 57 apps. Deel doesn't publish its own list of supported apps. Everything else goes back to manual removal.


-


**SCIM costs still apply:** The apps your IdP can provision usually need SCIM. Many apps only offer SCIM on their Enterprise plans.


-


**Fewer features than a dedicated tool:** Deel's FAQ says choosing apps per group only works with IdPs where Deel has an "enhanced" integration, such as Google and JumpCloud. It creates and removes accounts but doesn't manage roles inside each app.


-


**Shadow IT stays open:** Apps employees sign up for on their own never touch the IdP, so those accounts aren't removed.


-


**Price:** Access Management is only on Deel IT's top plan. Deel's pricing page lists Deel IT Scale at $149 per user per month, bundled with device management, endpoint protection and 24/7 IT support. AccessOwl's pricing page lists $6 per user per month, plus $2.50 for provisioning.


AccessOwl is another option if you run Deel. It's on the[Deel Marketplace](https://marketplace.deel.wtf/en/apps/access-owl) , integrates with 50+ other HR systems and syncs with your IdP. You get the same joined-up HR and IT setup, with wider app coverage and deeper automation.


## Corma


Corma calls itself a "license & access governance platform for modern IT teams." It began in SaaS spend management. Today most of what it ships is identity and access: onboarding, offboarding, access reviews and AI agents that act inside apps.


### What They Offer


Corma's workflow builder starts joiner, mover and leaver workflows from your HRIS, your identity provider or its API. Its 20+ HRIS integrations bring in employees, managers, and start and end dates. One example rule from Corma's 2026 changelog: when someone's termination date arrives, Corma asks the manager to confirm, then removes their accounts. Workflows can branch, so employees and external contractors follow different paths.


For apps without a usable API, Corma says its browser-based agents can do the work: "If an app has an interface, we can connect it." In Google Workspace, Corma can transfer a leaver's Drive, Calendar and Looker data to another employee and sign the user out of all Google sessions. Corma says its custom agents can be trained by demonstration, and its 2026 changelog adds an MCP server.


Spend features are still there. A browser extension on every plan detects the apps employees use, and renewal alerts and unused-license reports help you cut seats before contracts renew.


### Good For


Teams that want access management and license spend in one tool. If IT and finance share the SaaS budget, Corma puts offboarding, renewals and unused seats in the same place. Its free plan lets you try the discovery side before you buy. It also suits teams that track renewals in spreadsheets today and want each offboarding to free the license at the same time.


### Limitations


Much of the offboarding depth sits on the Pro plan. Corma's pricing page lists "Provisioning without APIs" and "Automated Access Token Revocation" under Pro.


Corma advertises 800+ integrations on Pro but doesn't publish which apps it can automatically deprovision. That makes its coverage hard to compare with other tools. Ask for a check against your own app list during a trial.


### Bottom Line


Corma fits teams that want access and spend handled in one place. If your main goal is removing leavers from every app, check which of your apps it removes automatically and which plan you'd need for that.


## YeshID


YeshID positions itself as an AI-native access control tool for small teams. It's free for teams under 20 users, and paid plans start at $9 per user per month. The product includes lifecycle automation, Shadow IT detection, and an AI assistant called Rae that helps configure policies and workflows. For a detailed comparison, see our[YeshID vs AccessOwl head-to-head](https://www.accessowl.com/alternatives/yeshid-vs-accessowl) .


### What They Offer


The free tier makes YeshID accessible if you're under 20 employees and trying to get basic access management in place without spending anything. You get lifecycle automation that connects to your HRIS, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Okta to handle provisioning and deprovisioning. Starting workflows from your HRIS needs the Business plan. Shadow IT visibility reads OAuth logs to detect unapproved applications.


The AI assistant (Rae) adds a conversational layer to tasks that should be straightforward configuration. Instead of directly setting up an approval workflow or defining who gets deprovisioned when, you're asking an AI to interpret your intent and configure settings on your behalf.


YeshID's docs list 158 apps, and 135 of them support deprovisioning. Every one connects through SCIM or a REST API, so the app needs an API and often the right plan. In YeshID's words, it can connect "If your application has a REST API & if you have the right subscription." Once you move beyond that set, you'll hit manual provisioning gaps.


### Good For


YeshID works for very early-stage companies under 20 employees that want a free or low-cost entry point into access management. If you're a 12-person startup with minimal budget and you need something better than a spreadsheet, the free tier gives you basic lifecycle automation without upfront cost. The product fits teams comfortable experimenting with lighter-weight tooling that may need replacement as they scale.


### Limitations


The AI layer creates problems where none should exist. Access decisions need to be explicit, auditable, and deterministic. When you offboard an employee, you want to know exactly which systems will revoke access and when, not ask an AI assistant to handle it and hope the interpretation matches your intent. For compliance requirements like SOC 2 or ISO 27001, auditors expect documented policies and clear evidence trails, not conversational AI logs.


YeshID relies on role-based access control (RBAC) instead of attribute-based access control (ABAC). RBAC works when you have five roles and straightforward permission structures. Once you grow past 50 employees with multiple departments, teams, and project-based access needs, RBAC becomes unmanageable. You end up with role explosion, where you're maintaining dozens of narrowly-defined roles just to handle normal access variations.


API connectors also follow each app's own plan. YeshID's Slack docs say creating or deactivating Slack accounts needs SCIM, which means Slack's Business+ or Enterprise Grid plan. Apps without a usable API become manual checklist tasks. Connecting a custom app means entering endpoint URLs, API tokens and SCIM URLs yourself.


## Cakewalk


Cakewalk markets itself on interface polish and integration numbers. The 5,600 supported applications claim appears throughout their materials, alongside customizable workflows and Agent Cake, its provisioning agent. Automated deprovisioning is recent: it arrived in December 2025. For a detailed comparison, see our[Cakewalk vs AccessOwl head-to-head](https://www.accessowl.com/alternatives/cakewalk-vs-accessowl) .


### What They Offer


The UI looks cleaner than most access management tools. Access requests, approval workflows, and policy configuration get presented through an interface that feels designed, not assembled from admin panels. If you're demoing tools to executives who care about visual presentation, Cakewalk makes a strong first impression.


A browser extension detects which applications employees are using. The policy builder lets you create custom workflows with multiple approval steps, conditional logic, and different paths based on application sensitivity or user role. You can define who approves what, when approvals escalate, and how requests get routed.


Agent Cake signs in to each supported app with a scoped service account and makes the change directly, so those apps don't need SCIM. A Slack assistant files access requests, and the open API allows custom integrations for internal tools or applications outside their supported list.


### Limitations


The 5,600 supported applications number misleads more than it informs. Having an application logo in a directory doesn't mean the tool can automatically provision or deprovision users in that application. Cakewalk's integration guides list 75 apps with automated provisioning and 64 with automated deprovisioning. Of the 75, 16 connect with a vendor API key and 59 sign in with a service account. For everything else, provisioning is a task for an admin or app owner by default. You're not getting automated deprovisioning across thousands of applications.


Customizable workflows transfer the configuration burden to you. Instead of opinionated defaults that handle common scenarios immediately, you're building workflows from scratch. This matters when you're the only IT person at your company. You don't have time to map out every approval chain, configure conditional logic for each application, and test edge cases. You need a tool that understands standard offboarding patterns and works without weeks of setup.


Outside Agent Cake's list, you'll still handle much of the actual access revocation manually. Cakewalk creates the task, routes it through approvals, and tracks status, but someone still needs to log into the application and disable the account. Leavers from the HRIS also start with a "Review offboarding" task that someone confirms before anything is removed. For offboarding automation, the fundamental test is whether the tool actually closes accounts without human intervention.


### Bottom Line


Cakewalk packages access management workflows attractively but doesn't deliver the automation depth needed for real offboarding at scale. If you're choosing tools based on how they look in a demo, Cakewalk wins. If you're choosing based on how many manual hours they eliminate from your offboarding process, the gap between supported applications and actual automation becomes the deciding factor.

## Why AccessOwl Is the Best Offboarding Automation Tool


Most offboarding tools stop at your identity provider and call it done. They disable an account in Okta or Google Workspace, send a completion notification, and mark the task complete. The problem is that disabling an IDP account doesn't actually revoke access to most SaaS applications. Active browser sessions stay logged in. Applications that allow username and password authentication continue working. API tokens remain valid. The employee's account shows "suspended" in your directory while they're still reading Slack messages and browsing your Notion workspace.


This isn't a hypothetical risk. Research shows that[50% of companies found](https://thehackernews.com/2024/05/new-research-warns-about-weak.html) former employees still accessing SaaS applications months after their departure. Separately,[63% of businesses](https://www.josys.com/article/top-saas-cybersecurity-risks) may have former employees with access to organizational data. These numbers reflect what happens when offboarding stops at the IDP layer instead of pushing through to actual application-level revocation.


### Access removed inside each app


We connect directly to each SaaS application through service accounts, APIs, and RPA to disable the account in that system, revoke session tokens, and force logouts. The user loses access to the actual application itself, beyond the SSO pathway that may or may not control their current session.


### Shadow IT included in every offboarding


Shadow IT discovery matters because you can't revoke what you don't know exists. Every access management tool claims to solve this, but most run a one-time scan or require you to manually add detected applications to a managed list. We continuously read OAuth logs from your identity provider and track every application employees authenticate into, whether you approved it or not. When someone leaves, these detected applications automatically enter the offboarding workflow alongside your managed stack. You're not hoping you remembered to check Loom, Miro, or whichever tool your team started using last month.


### Offboarding starts from your HRIS


HRIS integration removes the failure point where someone needs to remember that today is an employee's last day and manually trigger offboarding. We read termination dates directly from BambooHR, Rippling, Personio, and other systems. When that date arrives, deprovisioning starts automatically across every application the employee accessed. No ticket creation, no Slack reminder to HR, no manual checklist.


### Set up and run by HR and Ops, not only IT


You don't need IT certifications or API scripts to run AccessOwl. Connecting an app means inviting an integration account and giving it the right permissions. There are no endpoint URLs, API tokens or SCIM URLs to set up. That's why HR or Ops runs offboarding at many of the companies we work with. They start it from the HRIS or with one click, and app owners are notified for anything that needs a person.


At FinCompare, the Office Manager runs on- and offboarding:


> "It's a single click and every stakeholder gets the information they need."
>
>
> Robert Pötzsch, Office Manager, from[FinCompare's success story](https://www.accessowl.com/customers/fincompare)


### No SCIM or Enterprise plans needed


The real differentiation comes from working without SCIM. Other tools require you to pay for Enterprise plans across your entire SaaS stack just to get provisioning APIs. We connect through service accounts and direct integrations that function on standard business plans. When you're spending $12 per user monthly on a tool with 15 seats, you're not upgrading to a $50,000 annual Enterprise contract just to automate deprovisioning. We handle those applications anyway, using the same access methods your team uses manually but executed programmatically at scale.


### Assets move before the account closes


Asset reassignment prevents critical customer data from disappearing when an account closes. We automatically transfer document ownership, reassign tickets, and move shared resources to designated team members before deprovisioning the account. You control where assets go, and the system executes those transfers as part of the automated workflow.


## Final Thoughts on Automating Employee Offboarding


[Employee offboarding software](https://www.accessowl.com/use-cases/automate-onboarding-offboarding) should remove the manual work from your process, not create a prettier checklist that still requires you to log into 40 different applications. The tools that actually automate deprovisioning connect through service accounts and APIs that work on standard business plans, beyond Enterprise tiers with SCIM. Your choice comes down to whether you want to keep spending 3-5 hours per offboarding or whether you want the system to handle it automatically while you focus on projects that actually move your infrastructure forward. You can[scan your current access](https://www.accessowl.com/scan) to see how many former employees still show up with active accounts in your SaaS stack.


## FAQ


### Which offboarding automation tool works best for companies without SCIM access?


AccessOwl automates deprovisioning across 500+ SaaS applications without requiring SCIM or Enterprise plans. Most alternatives rely on SCIM protocols, which means you'd need to upgrade every tool to Enterprise tier just to get automated provisioning.


### I work in HR. How do I make sure all app access is revoked when an employee leaves?


Start from the system you already own: your HR platform. AccessOwl connects to HR systems like BambooHR, HiBob, Personio, Deel and Rippling, and to your Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. When you set an end date in the HR system, AccessOwl removes the person's access in each app on their last working day. You don't need IT certifications or scripts to set it up. Connecting an app means inviting an integration account, so many HR teams run offboarding themselves before there's a dedicated IT team.


### I run Operations and IT landed on my plate. How can I automate offboarding without an IT team?


Look for a tool that a non-technical person can set up and run. With AccessOwl, Ops managers start offboarding from the HR system or with one click. AccessOwl removes the person from every connected app and notifies app owners about anything that still needs a person. Every removal is logged, so you have the evidence ready when an access review or audit comes around. It works alongside the Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 account you already have, and it's built for companies of 30 to 1,000 people that don't want a full identity suite like Okta.


### How do I choose between offboarding tools if I have less than 20 employees?


YeshID offers a free tier for companies under 20 employees, while AccessOwl provides the most automation for organizations scaling past that point. If your primary concern is SaaS spend over security, Corma's finance-focused features might align better with your CFO's priorities.


### What happens to active browser sessions when I disable an employee's account in my IdP?


Disabling an account in Okta or Google Workspace doesn't kill active sessions in most SaaS applications. Employees can stay logged into Slack, AWS, or GitHub for hours or days afterward unless the tool actively revokes session tokens at the application level.


### Can offboarding automation handle Shadow IT applications my team uses without approval?


Tools that continuously scan OAuth logs from your identity provider will detect and include these hidden applications in offboarding workflows. Without this capability, you'll miss accounts in applications like Loom, Miro, or Notion that employees authenticated into without IT approval.


### When should I focus on asset reassignment over speed during offboarding?


You need asset reassignment before account closure whenever employees own customer data, open deals, active tickets, or shared documents. Without it, critical information disappears into closed accounts and becomes inaccessible to the rest of your team.
